pumac-2022-geometry-b-01.title: Parallel lines and angle sums
pumac-2022-geometry-b-01.body:
In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle ABC=180^\circ-32^\circ-60^\circ=88^\circ$, so $\angle ABE=\angle ABC-\angle EBC=88^\circ-25^\circ=63^\circ$.

Since $AD\parallel BE$, the angle between line $AB$ and line $AD$ equals the angle between $AB$ and $BE$. Depending on which side of $A$ the point $D$ lies on the parallel line, $\angle DAB$ is either $\angle ABE=63^\circ$ (alternate angles) or its supplement $180^\circ-63^\circ=117^\circ$.

The smallest possible value is $63^\circ$.

**Answer: 63**

pumac-2022-geometry-b-01.title: Check with the angles at E
pumac-2022-geometry-b-01.body:
$\angle BEC=180^\circ-25^\circ-32^\circ=123^\circ$, so $\angle BEA=57^\circ$ and, in $\triangle ABE$, $\angle ABE=180^\circ-60^\circ-57^\circ=63^\circ$, as before. If $D$ is chosen so that ray $AD$ points opposite to ray $BE$, then $\angle DAC=\angle BEC=123^\circ$ and $\angle DAB=123^\circ-60^\circ=63^\circ$; if ray $AD$ points the same way as ray $BE$, $\angle DAC=57^\circ$ and $\angle DAB=57^\circ+60^\circ=117^\circ$. The minimum is $63^\circ$.

**Answer: 63**

pumac-2022-geometry-b-02.title: Distance between tangency points
pumac-2022-geometry-b-02.body:
Two spheres of radii $r_1,r_2$ touching the plane and each other have centres $r_1+r_2$ apart. Take the plane through both centres perpendicular to the ground. The centres are at heights $r_1,r_2$ above the tangency points, so the horizontal distance $d$ between the tangency points satisfies
$$d^2+(r_1-r_2)^2=(r_1+r_2)^2,\qquad d=2\sqrt{r_1r_2}.$$
The three sides are $2\sqrt{48}=8\sqrt3$, $2\sqrt{60}=4\sqrt{15}$ and $2\sqrt{80}=8\sqrt5$, so the perimeter is
$$8\sqrt3+4\sqrt{15}+8\sqrt5\approx13.856+15.492+17.889=47.237.$$
To be rigorous: $13.85^2<192$, $15.49^2<240$, $17.88^2<320$ give a perimeter $>47.22$, and $13.86^2>192$, $15.50^2>240$, $17.89^2>320$ give a perimeter $<47.25<48$.

The largest integer smaller than the perimeter is $47$.

**Answer: 47**

pumac-2022-geometry-b-03.title: Right angle at P
pumac-2022-geometry-b-03.body:
Let $O=(0,0)$, $R=2022\sqrt3$ the radius of $\Gamma$, $Q$ the centre of $\Omega$ and $r$ its radius. Note $OA=6066=R\sqrt3$.

Orthogonality means the radii $OP$ and $QP$ are perpendicular, so $\triangle OPQ$ is right-angled at $P$ and $OQ=\sqrt{R^2+r^2}$. Since $A$ lies on the ray $OQ$ beyond $Q$ (as $Q$ is on the $x$-axis and $A$ on $\Omega$ on the far side), $OA=OQ+QA$:
$$\sqrt{R^2+r^2}+r=R\sqrt3\ \Longrightarrow\ R^2+r^2=3R^2-2\sqrt3Rr+r^2\ \Longrightarrow\ r=\frac{R}{\sqrt3}=2022 .$$
Then $\cos\angle OQP=\dfrac{QP}{OQ}=\dfrac{r}{\sqrt{R^2+r^2}}=\dfrac{2022}{4044}=\dfrac12$, so $\angle OQP=60^\circ$ and the central angle $\angle AQP=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$.

The minor arc $AP$ has length $\frac{120}{360}\cdot2\pi\cdot2022=1348\pi$, so $m=1348$, $n=1$ and $m+n=1349$.

**Answer: 1349**

pumac-2022-geometry-b-04.title: Smallest possible circle
pumac-2022-geometry-b-04.body:
Let the ellipse have semi-axes $R\ge r$, centre $O$ and $OA=OB=c_0$ with $c_0^2=R^2-r^2$, eccentricity $e=c_0/R$. The circle through $A,B,C$ has radius $\rho=\dfrac{AB}{2\sin\angle ACB}=\dfrac{c_0}{\sin\angle ACB}\ge c_0$, and its area equals the ellipse's area $\pi Rr$ iff $\rho^2=Rr$.

As $C$ runs around the ellipse, $\rho$ takes every value from its minimum up to arbitrarily large values (as $C$ approaches the major axis). The angle $\angle ACB$ is largest at an end of the minor axis, where it is $\ge90^\circ$ exactly when $c_0\ge r$, i.e. $e^2\ge\frac12$. For such $e$ the smallest circle has $\rho=c_0$ (when $\angle ACB=90^\circ$, i.e. $C$ on the circle with diameter $AB$), and a suitable $C$ exists iff $Rr\ge c_0^2$.

Dividing by $R^2$: $\sqrt{1-e^2}\ge e^2$, i.e. $e^4+e^2-1\le0$, which gives $e^2\le\dfrac{-1+\sqrt5}2\approx0.618$ (this is $\ge\frac12$, so it is consistent). The largest eccentricity therefore has
$$e^2=\frac{-1+\sqrt5}{2},$$
so $a=-1$, $b=5$, $c=2$ and $a^2+b^2+c^2=1+25+4=30$.

**Answer: 30**

pumac-2022-geometry-b-05.title: Roots of unity
pumac-2022-geometry-b-05.body:
Place the hexagon's vertices at the sixth roots of unity $\zeta^k$ ($\zeta=e^{i\pi/3}$) and let $P$ be the complex number $z$ with $|z|\le2$. Since $\prod_{k=0}^5(z-\zeta^k)=z^6-1$,
$$|PA||PB||PC||PD||PE||PF|=|z^6-1|\le|z|^6+1\le2^6+1=65.$$
Equality needs $|z|=2$ and $z^6$ to be a negative real, $z^6=-64$, which has $6$ solutions. So $M=65$, $N=6$ and $M+N^2=65+36=101$.

**Answer: 101**

pumac-2022-geometry-b-06.title: Angle chase, then law of sines
pumac-2022-geometry-b-06.body:
Take side length $1$. In the similarity $A\leftrightarrow B\leftrightarrow C$, $D\leftrightarrow E\leftrightarrow E$, $F\leftrightarrow D\leftrightarrow F$, the sides $DF,\ ED,\ EF$ correspond. Areas of similar triangles are proportional to the squares of corresponding sides, so $[ADF]=[BED]+[CEF]$ gives $DF^2=DE^2+EF^2$: $\angle DEF=90^\circ$.

Let $x=\angle BED=\angle CEF$ (corresponding angles). On line $BC$, $x+90^\circ+x=180^\circ$, so $x=45^\circ$. Thus $\triangle BED$ and $\triangle CEF$ have angles $60^\circ,45^\circ,75^\circ$. At $D$: $\angle ADF+\angle FDE+\angle BDE=180^\circ$ with $\angle ADF=45^\circ$ and $\angle BDE=75^\circ$ gives $\angle FDE=60^\circ$, so $\triangle DEF$ is $30$-$60$-$90$ with $EF=\sqrt3\,DE$.

Let $BE=u$, so $CE=1-u$. In $\triangle BED$ the side $BE$ is opposite the $75^\circ$ angle at $D$ and $DE$ is opposite the $60^\circ$ angle at $B$; similarly in $\triangle CEF$. By the law of sines
$$DE=\frac{u\sin60^\circ}{\sin75^\circ},\qquad EF=\frac{(1-u)\sin60^\circ}{\sin75^\circ}.$$
$EF=\sqrt3\,DE$ gives $1-u=\sqrt3u$, $u=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2}$. Then
$$DE=\frac{u\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}}=\frac{2\sqrt3-3}{\sqrt2},\qquad DE^2=\frac{21-12\sqrt3}{2}.$$
$[DEF]=\tfrac12\cdot DE\cdot\sqrt3DE=\frac{\sqrt3}2DE^2$ and $[ABC]=\frac{\sqrt3}4$, so
$$\frac{[ABC]}{[DEF]}=\frac1{2DE^2}=\frac1{21-12\sqrt3}=\frac{21+12\sqrt3}{441-432}=\frac{7+4\sqrt3}{3}.$$
Therefore $a+b+c+d=7+4+3+3=17$.

**Answer: 17**

pumac-2022-geometry-b-07.title: O is the circumcentre of XYZ
pumac-2022-geometry-b-07.body:
$X,Y,Z$ lie on the excircle, so $O$ is the circumcentre of $\triangle XYZ$ with circumradius $\rho=r_A$. The distance from the circumcentre to a side is $\rho|\cos(\text{opposite angle})|$.

**Angles of $\triangle XYZ$.** $\angle XOY=C$ (the radii $OX\perp BC$, $OY\perp CA$ and the angle at $C$ between $CB$ and the extension of $AC$ is $180^\circ-C$), so $\angle XZY=\frac C2$; similarly $\angle XYZ=\frac B2$; and $\angle YXZ=180^\circ-\frac B2-\frac C2=90^\circ+\frac A2$. Hence
$$h_1=\rho\cos\tfrac C2,\qquad h_3=\rho\cos\tfrac B2,\qquad h_2=\rho\sin\tfrac A2 .$$

**Numbers.** With $a=8$, $b=7$, $c=5$, $s=10$: $\cos A=\frac{49+25-64}{70}=\frac17$, $\cos B=\frac{64+25-49}{80}=\frac12$, $\cos C=\frac{64+49-25}{112}=\frac{11}{14}$. The area is $K=\sqrt{10\cdot2\cdot3\cdot5}=10\sqrt3$ and $\rho=r_A=\frac{K}{s-a}=5\sqrt3$, so $\rho^2=75$. Then
$$\cos^2\tfrac C2=\frac{1+\cos C}2=\frac{25}{28},\quad\cos^2\tfrac B2=\frac34,\quad\sin^2\tfrac A2=\frac{1-\cos A}2=\frac37,$$
$$h_1^2+h_2^2+h_3^2=75\left(\frac{25}{28}+\frac{21}{28}+\frac{12}{28}\right)=75\cdot\frac{29}{14}=\frac{2175}{14}.$$
Since $2175=3\cdot5^2\cdot29$ is coprime to $14$, $m+n=2175+14=2189$.

**Answer: 2189**

pumac-2022-geometry-b-08.title: Radical axis and a root-bc inversion
pumac-2022-geometry-b-08.body:
A circle tangent to line $AB$ that passes through $B\in AB$ is tangent to $AB$ at $B$; so $\omega_1$ touches $AB$ at $B$ and $AC$, and $\omega_2$ touches $AC$ at $C$ and $AB$. Both centres $O_1,O_2$ lie on the bisector $\ell$ of $\angle A$, so $\ell$ is the line of centres and $XY$ (the radical axis) is perpendicular to $\ell$ at its midpoint $P$, with $AX=AY$.

**$AX$.** Reflect in $\ell$ and then invert about $A$ with radius $\sqrt{AB\cdot AC}=\sqrt{140}$. Call this map $\Phi$. It swaps $B\leftrightarrow C$ and the lines $AB\leftrightarrow AC$, so it carries $\omega_1$ to $\omega_2$ and $\omega_2$ to $\omega_1$, hence it permutes $\{X,Y\}$. The reflection alone swaps $X$ and $Y$ (they are mirror images in $\ell$). So either $\Phi(X)=Y$, which means the inversion fixes $X$ and $AX^2=140$, or $\Phi(X)=X$, which means the inversion sends $X$ to $Y$ and $AX\cdot AY=140$. Since $AX=AY$, in both cases $AX^2=140$.

**$AP$.** $\cos A=\frac{100+196-256}{2\cdot140}=\frac17$, so $\tan\frac A2=\frac{\sqrt3}2$ and $\cos\frac A2=\frac2{\sqrt7}$. The radii are $r_1=AB\tan\frac A2=5\sqrt3$, $r_2=AC\tan\frac A2=7\sqrt3$, and $AO_1=\frac{AB}{\cos(A/2)}=5\sqrt7$, $AO_2=7\sqrt7$, so $O_1O_2=2\sqrt7$. Let $s$ be the signed distance from $O_1$ to $P$ along $\ell$ (positive towards $O_2$). Then $r_1^2-s^2=r_2^2-(s-2\sqrt7)^2$, giving $75=147-28+4\sqrt7s$, so $s=-\frac{11}{\sqrt7}$ and
$$AP=5\sqrt7-\frac{11\sqrt7}{7}=\frac{24\sqrt7}7 .$$

**Perimeter.** $XP^2=AX^2-AP^2=140-\frac{576}7=\frac{404}7$, so $XY=2XP=4\sqrt{\frac{101}7}$ and the perimeter is $2\sqrt{140}+XY=4\sqrt{35}+4\sqrt{\frac{101}{7}}$. Squaring,
$$560+\frac{1616}7+32\sqrt{505}=\frac{5536+224\sqrt{505}}7 .$$
So $a+b+c+d=5536+224+505+7=6272$ (numerically $1509.97$).

**Answer: 6272**
